title: Height & Diameter

why_it_exists.problem: To understand the bounding dimensions of a hierarchical structure (like maximum latency, longest decision path, or physical rendering size), you need to measure its extremities.
why_it_exists.better_idea: The 'height' measures the longest path from the root to a leaf, dictating maximum recursive depth. The 'diameter' measures the longest path between ANY two nodes in the tree, representing the absolute maximum distance across the structure.

mental_model.intuition: Height is reaching straight down as far as possible. Diameter is stretching your arms out to the left and right as far as possible.
mental_model.description: A node calculates its height bottom-up: it asks its children for their heights, takes the maximum, and adds 1 for itself. While doing this, the node simultaneously calculates its local diameter (left child's height + right child's height) and updates a global tracker if its local stretch is the widest seen so far.
mental_model.repeated_decision: My height is 1 + max(left, right). My local diameter is left + right. Is my diameter the new global max?

explanation:
Height and diameter are intimately connected. In fact, the most efficient way to find the diameter is to piggyback it onto a standard height-calculation function.

The height of a node is defined as the number of edges on the longest downward path from the node to a leaf. A leaf has a height of 0. A null pointer is mathematically considered to have a height of -1 (or 0, depending on edge vs. node counting conventions). The recursive formula is `height = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))`.

The diameter of a tree is the length of the longest path between any two nodes. This path may or may not pass through the root! However, the path MUST pass through *some* node acting as the peak (the highest node on that specific path). For any given node acting as a peak, the longest path passing through it is exactly `height(node.left) + height(node.right) + 2` (assuming heights of leaves are 0). 

By running a post-order traversal to calculate height, you can pause at every node, calculate its local diameter, update a global `max_diameter` variable, and then return the height upward. This solves both problems simultaneously in O(N) time.

key_points.title: Post-order synthesis
key_points.detail: Calculating height fundamentally requires Post-order traversal. A parent cannot know its height until the children have completely computed and returned theirs.

key_points.title: Diameter doesn't always include the root
key_points.detail: In a highly unbalanced tree, the longest path might be entirely contained within a massive left subtree, completely ignoring the absolute root.

common_mistakes.title: The O(N^2) trap
common_mistakes.explanation: A common mistake is writing a `diameter` function that internally calls a separate `height` function on `node.left` and `node.right`. Because `height` traverses the whole subtree, doing this at every node results in O(N^2) time. You must compute diameter *inside* the height function to achieve O(N).

common_mistakes.title: Assuming the diameter passes through the root
common_mistakes.explanation: Don't just calculate `height(root.left) + height(root.right)`. You must check the local diameter at *every single node* in the tree.

recall_questions.q: What is the recursive formula for the height of a binary tree node?
Why is it inefficient to call a separate `height()` helper function from within a recursive `diameter()` function?
recall_questions.answer: Because `height()` traverses the entire subtree, calling it at every node recalculates the same heights repeatedly, degrading the time complexity to O(N^2).

recall_questions.q: Does the longest path (diameter) of a binary tree always pass through the root node?
recall_questions.answer: No. In an unbalanced tree, the longest path might be entirely contained within one of the subtrees, acting like an umbrella completely underneath the root.

oa_questions.question: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of the diameter of the tree.
oa_questions.answer: Create a `max_d = 0` variable. Write a `dfs(node)` function that returns 0 if null. Let `left = dfs(node.left)` and `right = dfs(node.right)`. Update `max_d = max(max_d, left + right)`. Return `1 + max(left, right)`. Finally, return `max_d`.
oa_questions.approach: Piggyback the diameter calculation onto a standard post-order height calculation to achieve O(N) time.

oa_questions.question: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth.
oa_questions.answer: If root is null, return 0. Otherwise, return 1 + max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right)).
oa_questions.approach: This is the purest application of the post-order synthesis mental model.

engineering_examples.title: UI Layout Engines
engineering_examples.problem: Calculating the total bounding box size of a nested UI component (like a flexbox container).
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: The layout engine performs a post-order traversal to calculate the height and width of children before it can determine the final dimensions of the parent container.

engineering_examples.title: Network Latency Analysis
engineering_examples.problem: Finding the maximum possible communication delay in a hierarchical routing network.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: The diameter of the routing tree represents the absolute worst-case hop count (latency) between any two nodes in the network.
